newsitem.title: JAPAN: LUGE-AMONG THE COWS, GOATS AND BUFFALO - INDIA'S FIRST LUGER.
newsitem.headline: LUGE-AMONG THE COWS, GOATS AND BUFFALO - INDIA'S FIRST LUGER.

text.p: Dodging cows, goats and water buffalo, a young sports student lying flat out on a fibreglass sled rolled down a sideroad last year outside the northern Indian city of Chandigar.
Ragged children and women bearing bundles on their heads stood transfixed, unaware they were witnessing the birth of the 2002 Indian Olympic luge team.
At least Gunther Lemmerer, coach of a multi-national group of lugers competing at a World Cup meeting in Nagano beginning Saturday, hopes so.

Hired nine years ago by the International Luge Federation (FIL) to coach the sports "orphan" athletes, Lemmerer travels to far-flung places like Chandigar to introduce luge to young people who may never even have seen snow.

One of the two Indian athletes he picked to attend training camps in Europe from among more than two dozen Chandigar hopefuls served as a forerunner at the world championships in Igls, Austria, last month.

Lemmerer's 21 other athletes in Igls hailed from 12 countries, comprising Belgium, Bermuda, Britain, Bosnia, Estonia, Greece, Liechtenstein, New Zealand, Norway, South Korea, Taiwan and the Virgin Islands.
In Nagano, where this weekend's luge events will be held at the same Spiral track as next years Olympics, he has 13 athletes from seven countries.

"We wanted to collect these individual athletes just to give them direction because the risk was pretty high since they came without much coaching or background in the sport," said Lemmerer, a 14-year veteran of the Austrian national team.
"It was a serious risk for the FIL to let them compete because some didn't really know how to slide," he added.

Because until recently no international qualifying standards were imposed on lugers, most of Lemmerer's athletes were drawn to the sport by the lure of the Olympics. Without that incentive, they might just as easily have taken up bungee jumping or white-water rafting, he said.
None has ever stood on a podium. They lodge in dormitories while more established teams check into hotels. But the FIL group, as they are officially known, has slowly gained respect.
Qualifying standards imposed in 1993 required competitors to qualify for each international event by completing a training run within 10 percent of the top training times.
Lemmerer and his athletes have since instigated even tougher standards, cutting the margin to seven percent.
Lemmerer says his mixed team sometimes functions even more harmoniously than a regular national squad where athletes must compete among themselves for a limited number of places.

And their multi-ethnicity sometimes comes in handy. Last year while rushing across Estonia to catch a ferry to Sweden to keep up with a tight World Cup schedule, Lemmerer was pulled over by Estonian police for speeding.

After explaining that the car contained the Estonian national luge team -- which consisted of one woman who had been conscripted as translator -- Lemmerer pleaded for a police escort. In exchange for 100 German marks and a tankful of petrol, the police led the team 195 kms to Tallinn with blue lights flashing.

Although Lemmerer is always open to invitations to introduce his sport to the uninitiated, he particularly wants to reach Asian audiences to ensure that the Nagano track will be used after next years Olympics.
China could possibly join Japan, South Korea and Taiwan to make up the four countries required for the sport to be admitted to the Asian Winter Games, he said.
"If they call me, I will come," he said.
